description: We're Sambhar Watch, two high-school students from Jaipur, India. Our project, Sambhar Watch, uses NISAR radar to track surface water at Sambhar Lake, a protected Ramsar wetland 70 km from home, checked against Sentinel-2 images. Lokesh C. led the project and data analysis (Python, radar processing, validation). Bhagya M. did research, testing and review. We made the presentation together. Our team is complete.
summary:
Sambhar Watch is a free, open-source website that uses NISAR, a new NASA–ISRO radar satellite, to track how the water in Sambhar Lake changes through the year. Sambhar is India's largest inland salt lake and a protected wetland about 70 km from our home in Jaipur.

Normal satellite photos struggle here: monsoon clouds hide the lake, and white salt crust can be hard to tell apart from shallow water. Radar sees through clouds, but in radar images flat salt crust can look as dark as water.

We tested a simple fix: count a spot as water only if it looks dark AND its radar signal changes between two passes 12 days apart. We checked this against 177 points labelled from normal satellite photos. It scored 68%, compared with 58% using darkness alone. Inside our mapped lake outline, the estimated water area fell from about 91 to 56 km² between August and October 2026, and this drop appeared in all 12 settings we tested.

On the website you pick a date, see the detected water, and compare it with a photo from a nearby date. We show both methods' results and explain their errors and limits openly.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sambhar Watch is a website that estimates how much surface water is in Sambhar Lake, India's largest inland salt lake, about 70 km from our home in Jaipur. You pick a date and see a map of where the radar detects water, plus a chart of how the estimated water area changed over the year. You can also compare the radar map with a normal satellite photo from a nearby date.

WHY THIS LAKE IS HARD TO WATCH

Sambhar is a protected wetland (a "Ramsar site") where many birds feed. In 2019 more than 18,000 birds died there from a disease linked to the lake's condition. A salt industry also uses part of the lake. Normal satellite photos often fail here for two reasons: monsoon clouds block the view, and dry white salt crust can look like water, or water can look like salt.

HOW IT WORKS

We used NISAR, a new NASA–ISRO radar satellite. Radar sends its own signal and can see through clouds, day or night. We used two things the radar measures:

1. Brightness: smooth, calm surfaces like water reflect the signal away, so they look dark. The problem is that flat salt crust also looks dark, so brightness alone can't tell them apart.

2. Coherence: compares the radar signal from two passes 12 days apart. Open water usually gives low coherence because its surface keeps changing; stable dry surfaces like salt crust usually stay coherent. Low coherence alone doesn't prove water, so we use it together with brightness.

Our rule: a spot counts as water when it is dark AND has low coherence. Dark but coherent usually means salt crust or dry ground, so it is removed.

We used 24 radar images taken between November 2025 and November 2026, all free from NASA's archive.

WHAT WE FOUND

- Inside our mapped lake outline, the estimated water area fell from about 91 km² in mid-August to about 56 km² in mid-October 2026, a drop of about 35 km² after the monsoon.

- Using brightness alone, the estimated drop is much smaller: about 10 km² (125 → 115 km²), because brightness counts much of the new salt crust as water.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

- We picked 177 points inside the lake and labelled each one as water, salt crust or land by looking at normal satellite photos (Sentinel-2). Then we compared those labels with what the radar said. Our method scored 68%, against 58% for brightness alone. (We used "balanced accuracy", which counts water and non-water points equally, so a method can't score well just by saying "water" everywhere.)

- [The rule's cut-off values were fixed before the check points were labelled.]

- We tried 12 different combinations of the two cut-off values. The August-to-October drop appeared in all 12. That shows the result is consistent across those settings, not that the exact size of the drop is proven.

- Trade-off: in our check, brightness alone found most real water but also called most salt crust water. Our method rarely mistook crust for water but missed some real water, especially when the lake was full in January. The two methods give different estimates, and neither is a proven limit on the true area, so the app shows both.

HOW WE ARE DIFFERENT FROM WHAT ALREADY EXISTS

- Global water maps from normal satellite photos (like the JRC Global Surface Water map) cannot see through monsoon clouds and can confuse white salt crust with water. The JRC record we used ends in 2021.

- Many radar water-mapping tools rely mainly on brightness. At a salt lake that is a problem, because flat salt crust can look as dark as water.

- Published satellite studies of Sambhar (for example Singh et al., 2025, and the NRSC-ISRO / VIT-AP study) use optical images, which clouds block. NISAR passes every 12 days, through clouds.

- Combining brightness and coherence is not new: Festa et al. (2026, Remote Sensing) used it with yearly Sentinel-1 composites to map permanent water in dry regions. We apply and test the idea on a salt lake, date by date, with NISAR.

What Sambhar Watch adds:

1. It uses NISAR, a radar satellite launched in 2025 whose data only became publicly available this year.

2. It tests whether brightness plus coherence can tell water from salt crust at a real salt lake, and measures how well it works.

3. It shows how reliable it is: 177 check points, 12 settings tested, and limits stated openly.

4. It separates the salt-works zone from the rest of the lake.

5. It is built for non-experts: pick a date, see the estimated water, compare it with a normal photo.

WHO IT HELPS

Wetland managers, researchers and bird-watching groups could use it to see every 12 days whether the lake is drying fast, even under clouds. The data and code are free, and the method could be tested at other salt lakes.

TOOLS

Python for the data processing, NASA's Earthdata and ASF archive for the radar data, Sentinel-2 photos via Microsoft Planetary Computer for checking, Leaflet and Chart.js for the interactive map and chart, and GitHub Pages to host it free. We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code) to write much of the code under our direction. We chose the lake and the method, drew the lake outlines, labelled the 177 check points and checked every result.

LIMITS WE ARE OPEN ABOUT

- Only about one year of data, because NISAR launched in July 2025, so we don't predict future trends.

- We drew the lake outline by hand, and it misses about 11 km² of the lake's western edge. Adding it does not reverse the August-to-October drop, but it does change the absolute areas, so our numbers apply to our mapped outline.

- Our method misses some real water, especially when the lake is full. The 177 check points are close together in space and time, so they may not be fully independent tests.

- Coherence can also be low for reasons other than water (weak signal, noise, moisture changes).

https://github.com/lokesh09s/sambhar-watch (Our code repository)
